metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Companion for GCP Networking Fundamentals - covers VPC networks, subnets, firewall rules, load balancing, Cloud VPN, Cloud Interconnect, Cloud NAT, Cloud DNS, and Private Google Access.

question.title: VPC Network Fundamentals
question.scenario: Your company is starting a new project on Google Cloud and needs to set up isolated network resources for different environments (development, staging, production).
question.question-text: What is the primary characteristic of a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network in Google Cloud?

choices.choice: A regional network limited to a single geographic area
A global, private, isolated virtual network that spans all GCP regions
A physical network within Google's data centers
A public network shared between multiple GCP customers

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How does the scope of a GCP VPC compare to VPCs in other cloud providers? Think about whether it is tied to a single region or something broader.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A Google Cloud VPC is a global, private, isolated virtual network that spans all GCP regions automatically. This global scope means you can create subnets in different regions within the same VPC and resources can communicate via internal IP addresses without extra configuration. Option B is wrong because VPCs are global, not regional. Option C is wrong because VPCs are software-defined virtual networks, not physical infrastructure. Option D is wrong because each VPC is private and isolated to a single customer project.

ul.li: VPCs are global resources while subnets are regional. This means a single VPC can contain subnets in us-central1, europe-west1, and asia-east1 simultaneously, and VMs in those subnets communicate over Google's private backbone using internal IPs.

Every GCP project starts with a default VPC that has auto-mode subnets pre-created in every region. For production workloads, Google recommends custom-mode VPCs to control IP allocation and avoid range conflicts with on-premises networks.

VPC networks are isolated by default with no transitive peering. Two VPCs in the same project cannot communicate unless explicitly connected via VPC Peering, Shared VPC, Cloud VPN, or Private Service Connect.
The global nature of GCP VPCs is a key differentiator from AWS VPCs (which are regional) and is frequently tested on certification exams.

question.title: Subnet Modes
question.scenario: You are creating a new VPC network and need to decide how IP address ranges will be allocated across regions.
question.question-text: What is the difference between auto mode and custom mode VPC networks?

choices.choice: Auto mode uses public IPs; custom mode uses private IPs
Auto mode creates subnets automatically in each region; custom mode requires manual subnet creation
Auto mode is for production; custom mode is for development only
Auto mode is free; custom mode has additional charges

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider how subnets get created in each mode. Auto mode handles subnet provisioning for you in every region, while custom mode gives you explicit control over which regions have subnets and what IP ranges they use.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Auto mode VPC networks automatically create one subnet per region using predefined IP ranges from the 10.128.0.0/9 block, assigning a /20 range to each region. Custom mode VPCs start with no subnets and require you to manually create them with IP ranges you specify. Option A is wrong because both modes use private IPs for subnets. Option B reverses the recommendation: custom mode is actually preferred for production. Option D is wrong because pricing depends on resources deployed, not the VPC mode. Custom mode is recommended for production to avoid IP range conflicts with on-premises or peered networks.

ul.li: Auto mode subnets draw from 10.128.0.0/9 and assign a /20 per region (4,096 IPs each). As Google adds regions, new auto-mode subnets appear automatically, which can create unintended IP overlaps with on-premises ranges or peered VPCs.

You can convert an auto mode VPC to custom mode (one-way operation), which is a common migration path when teams outgrow the default setup. Custom mode lets you choose exact CIDR blocks, avoiding waste and overlap.

Custom mode is required when using VPC Peering or Shared VPC in production, because overlapping IP ranges between peered networks cause routing failures. Plan IP allocation carefully using a CIDR scheme that accounts for all connected networks.
The default VPC created with every new GCP project is auto mode. Deleting or converting it to custom mode is a recommended first step in enterprise landing zone designs.

question.title: Subnet IP Ranges
question.scenario: Your network team needs to plan IP address allocation for a new custom mode VPC that will host Kubernetes clusters requiring large IP ranges for pods and services.
question.question-text: What feature allows you to assign additional IP ranges to a subnet beyond the primary range?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP subnets can carry more than one CIDR block. The additional blocks are called secondary ranges, and they are essential for GKE clusters that need separate IP space for pods and services.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Secondary IP ranges (alias IP ranges) let you assign additional CIDR blocks to a subnet beyond its primary range. These secondary ranges are commonly used with GKE to provide dedicated IP space for pods and services without consuming primary subnet addresses. Option A (IP forwarding) enables a VM to send and receive packets with non-matching source/destination IPs, used for NAT or routing appliances. Option B (subnet expansion) lets you widen the primary range but does not add separate ranges. Option C (network peering) connects two VPCs but does not add IP ranges to a subnet.

ul.li: The primary range provides internal IPs for VM network interfaces. Secondary ranges provide alias IPs that are assigned to containers, pods, or additional services running on those VMs without consuming primary addresses.

VPC-native GKE clusters require two secondary ranges per subnet: one for pod IPs and one for service IPs. A typical cluster might use a /14 for pods (over 250,000 IPs) and a /20 for services (4,096 IPs), so careful CIDR planning is critical.

Alias IP ranges are advertised as subnet routes within the VPC, meaning other VMs and peered networks can reach pod IPs directly without NAT. This is a key advantage of VPC-native clusters over routes-based clusters.
You can add secondary ranges to an existing subnet without downtime, but you cannot remove a secondary range that is in use by a GKE cluster. Plan ranges generously to avoid costly cluster rebuilds.

question.title: Firewall Rule Basics
question.scenario: You deployed a web application on a Compute Engine VM but users cannot access it from the internet.
question.question-text: What type of VPC firewall rule is needed to allow incoming traffic to a VM?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Firewall rules have two directions: ingress controls traffic coming into a VM, and egress controls traffic leaving. Since users need to reach your VM, you need a rule that explicitly permits inbound connections.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: To allow incoming traffic to a VM, you need an ingress allow rule specifying the allowed source ranges, protocols, and ports. By default, GCP VPCs have an implied deny-all ingress rule and an implied allow-all egress rule. Option A would block traffic, not allow it. Option B controls outbound traffic from the VM, which does not help users reach it. Option D defines routing paths for packets but does not control whether traffic is permitted or blocked. For a web application, you would typically create an ingress allow rule for TCP ports 80 and 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0.

ul.li: GCP firewall rules are stateful: when an ingress allow rule permits a connection, the return traffic for that session is automatically allowed without a separate egress rule. This simplifies configuration compared to stateless ACLs.

The default VPC includes pre-populated rules such as default-allow-ssh (TCP 22), default-allow-rdp (TCP 3389), default-allow-icmp, and default-allow-internal. Custom VPCs start with only the implied deny-all ingress and allow-all egress rules.

Firewall rules are applied at the VM level, not at the subnet or network perimeter. Each rule specifies targets (all instances, tagged instances, or service-account-based instances) and is enforced by the hypervisor regardless of how many NICs or subnets are involved.
For troubleshooting, use Firewall Rules Logging or the Connectivity Tests tool to verify which rules are matching or blocking specific traffic flows to your VM.

question.title: Firewall Rule Targets
question.scenario: You have multiple web servers and database servers in your VPC. You need to create firewall rules that apply only to web servers.
question.question-text: What is the recommended method to target specific VMs with firewall rules?

choices.choice: Create separate VPC networks for each server type
Specify individual IP addresses in each rule
Use network tags or service accounts
Use VM instance names in firewall rules

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP firewall rules support flexible targeting mechanisms that apply dynamically as VMs are added or removed. Network tags and service accounts are the two recommended approaches for scoping rules to specific groups of instances.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Network tags and service accounts are the recommended ways to target VMs with firewall rules. Tags are user-defined strings you attach to VM instances, while service accounts provide identity-based targeting tied to IAM. Both approaches let rules apply dynamically to new VMs that match the criteria. Option A is overly complex and creates unnecessary network isolation overhead. Option C is fragile because IP addresses change when VMs are recreated or autoscaled. Option D is not supported; GCP firewall rules cannot target VMs by instance name. Between the two correct approaches, service accounts are considered more secure for production environments.

ul.li: Service account-based targeting is more secure because changing a VM's service account requires the iam.serviceAccounts.actAs permission, which is tightly controlled. Network tags can be modified by anyone with compute.instances.setTags permission, making them easier to misconfigure or abuse.

A single firewall rule can target instances by tag or by service account, but not both simultaneously. Rules can also target all instances in the network if no tag or service account filter is specified.

Network tags are case-sensitive strings (e.g., "web-server" and "Web-Server" are different tags). Tags are also used by routes to scope custom static routes to specific VMs, making them a dual-purpose network primitive.

In Shared VPC environments, service account-based rules are strongly preferred because service accounts are project-level resources managed by IAM, whereas tags are instance-level metadata that any project contributor might change.

question.title: Firewall Rule Priority
question.scenario: You have two firewall rules: one allows SSH from all sources with priority 1000, and another denies all traffic from a specific IP range with priority 900.
question.question-text: Which rule takes precedence when traffic from the specific IP range attempts SSH access?

choices.choice: The rules cancel each other out
The allow rule with priority 1000 takes precedence
Both rules are evaluated and the allow wins
The deny rule with priority 900 takes precedence

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP firewall rules are evaluated by priority number, where a lower number means higher precedence. When two rules could match the same traffic, the one with the lower priority value wins and the other is never evaluated.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firewall rules are evaluated strictly by priority, with lower numbers having higher precedence. The deny rule at priority 900 is evaluated before the allow rule at priority 1000, so SSH traffic from the specific IP range is denied. Option A is wrong because rules do not cancel each other; only the highest-priority matching rule applies. Option B is wrong because 1000 is a lower precedence than 900. Option C is wrong because GCP uses first-match semantics, not a combined evaluation. Once the priority-900 deny rule matches, evaluation stops and the traffic is blocked.

ul.li: Priority values range from 0 (highest precedence) to 65535 (lowest). The default implied deny-all ingress rule has priority 65535, and the implied allow-all egress rule has priority 65534. Custom rules should use priorities between 0 and 65534.

When two rules share the same priority and both match, deny takes precedence over allow. This tie-breaking behavior is a safety net, but relying on it is poor practice; use distinct priorities for clarity.

A common pattern is to set a broad deny rule at a moderate priority (e.g., 900) and then create more specific allow rules at higher priority (lower number, e.g., 800) for trusted sources. This implements a default-deny posture with explicit exceptions.

Hierarchical firewall policies (at org or folder level) are evaluated before VPC-level rules. A hierarchical rule with action "goto_next" delegates to the next level, while allow or deny at the hierarchy level takes final precedence over any VPC rule.

question.title: Load Balancer Types Overview
question.scenario: Your company needs to distribute incoming web traffic across multiple VM instances in different regions for a globally accessible application.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud load balancer type is best suited for global HTTP/HTTPS traffic distribution?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For HTTP/HTTPS workloads that serve users across multiple regions, you need a load balancer that operates globally and understands Layer 7 protocols. Think about which GCP load balancer provides a single anycast IP with content-aware routing.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Global external Application Load Balancer (formerly HTTP(S) Load Balancer) is purpose-built for distributing global HTTP/HTTPS traffic. It provides a single anycast IP address, SSL termination, URL-based content routing, and automatic failover to the nearest healthy backend region. Option A handles TCP/UDP at Layer 4 and is regional, not global. Option C is for internal-only traffic within a VPC. Option D is regional and internal, suitable for microservices behind a private frontend but not for internet-facing global traffic. The Global external ALB also integrates natively with Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor.

ul.li: The Global external ALB uses Google's global anycast network: client requests enter at the nearest Google edge point of presence and are routed over Google's private backbone to the closest healthy backend, minimizing latency and maximizing throughput.

URL maps enable content-based routing so a single load balancer can direct /api/* to one backend service and /static/* to another, or even route by HTTP headers. This eliminates the need for multiple load balancers for a single domain.

Native integration with Cloud CDN caches responses at edge locations, and Cloud Armor security policies provide DDoS protection and WAF rules. Google-managed SSL certificates automate certificate provisioning and renewal.

The Premium network service tier is required for global load balancing with anycast IPs. The Standard tier only supports regional external Application Load Balancers with region-specific IP addresses.

question.title: Backend Services
question.scenario: You are configuring an Application Load Balancer and need to define where traffic should be sent based on health checks.
question.question-text: What component of a load balancer defines the group of backends and their health check configuration?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: In GCP load balancer architecture, one specific component groups your backend instances together and associates a health check with them. This component also defines the load balancing algorithm and session affinity settings.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A backend service defines a logical group of backends (managed instance groups, unmanaged instance groups, or NEGs), their health check configuration, session affinity, and the load balancing distribution algorithm. Traffic is routed only to backends that pass health checks. Option A (target proxy) terminates client connections and forwards them based on URL map rules. Option C (URL map) defines routing rules that map URL paths to backend services but does not define the backends themselves. Option D (forwarding rule) binds an external IP and port to the target proxy, serving as the entry point for traffic. Together these four components form the load balancer pipeline: forwarding rule, target proxy, URL map, backend service.

ul.li: Backend services support three balancing modes: UTILIZATION (distribute based on backend CPU usage), RATE (distribute based on requests per second), and CONNECTION (distribute based on concurrent connections). The mode determines how the load balancer spreads traffic across backends.

Each backend service references exactly one health check. Health check probes originate from Google's dedicated IP ranges (130.211.0.0/22 and 35.191.0.0/16), so firewall rules must allow traffic from these ranges to the backend port.

Backend services can span multiple regions for global load balancers. A single backend service might include MIGs in us-central1, europe-west1, and asia-southeast1, with the load balancer routing users to the nearest healthy region automatically.

Capacity scaler (0.0 to 1.0) on each backend within a service lets you gradually shift traffic during migrations or canary deployments. Setting it to 0 drains the backend without removing it from the configuration.

question.title: URL Maps and Routing
question.scenario: You want to route requests to /api/* to one set of backends and /static/* to another set of backends using the same load balancer.
question.question-text: Which load balancer component enables content-based routing to different backend services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Content-based routing requires a component that inspects the request URL and decides which backend service should handle it. In GCP, this routing logic is defined declaratively in a configuration resource that maps URL patterns to backends.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: URL maps define rules that route incoming requests to different backend services based on the URL host and path. They support host rules (routing by domain name), path matchers (routing by URL path prefix or exact match), and a default backend service for unmatched requests. Option A (health check) verifies backend availability but plays no role in routing decisions. Option B (forwarding rule) maps an IP and port to a target proxy and does not inspect request content. Option C (target proxy) terminates connections and passes requests to the URL map but does not define routing logic itself. URL maps are the central routing brain of the Application Load Balancer.

ul.li: Path matchers support prefix matches (/api/*), exact matches (/health), and regex matches for complex patterns. Host rules let you serve api.example.com and www.example.com from the same load balancer IP but route to different backend services.

Advanced traffic management features include header-based routing, query parameter-based routing, traffic splitting (e.g., 90/10 canary), URL rewrites, and request/response header transformations, all configured within the URL map.

Each URL map must have a default service that handles requests not matching any explicit rule. Misconfiguring or omitting the default service causes 404 errors for unmatched paths, which is a common setup mistake.
URL maps are only used by Application Load Balancers (Layer 7). Network Load Balancers (Layer 4) do not use URL maps because they forward raw TCP/UDP connections without inspecting HTTP content.

question.title: Internal Load Balancing
question.scenario: Your application has a frontend tier that needs to communicate with a backend database tier. Both tiers are within the same VPC and should not be exposed to the internet.
question.question-text: Which load balancer type should you use for internal-only traffic within a VPC?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When traffic must stay entirely within your VPC and never touch the public internet, you need a load balancer that uses a private IP address as its frontend. GCP offers internal variants of both Application and Network load balancers for this purpose.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Internal passthrough Network Load Balancer (formerly Internal TCP/UDP Load Balancer) distributes traffic among backends using a private IP address accessible only within your VPC. It is ideal for internal tiers such as databases, caches, or microservices that should not be internet-facing. Option A (Cloud CDN) is a caching service, not a load balancer. Options B and C are external load balancers that expose public IPs to the internet, which violates the internal-only requirement. The internal passthrough NLB preserves the original client IP because it does not proxy connections, making it suitable for protocols that need source IP visibility.

ul.li: Internal load balancers are regional resources, meaning backends must be in the same region as the load balancer. For multi-region internal traffic distribution, you would need one internal LB per region with DNS-based or application-level routing between them.

The internal passthrough NLB uses Andromeda, Google's software-defined networking stack, to perform load balancing entirely in software at the hypervisor level. This means there is no single proxy bottleneck and the load balancer scales automatically with traffic.

GCP also offers an Internal Application Load Balancer (Layer 7) for internal HTTP/HTTPS workloads that need content-based routing, header manipulation, or TLS termination. Choose the internal ALB when you need URL-map routing; choose the internal passthrough NLB for raw TCP/UDP.

Internal load balancer IPs can be used as next hops in custom static routes, enabling patterns like hub-and-spoke routing through centralized firewall appliances or NAT instances deployed behind an internal NLB.

question.title: Cloud VPN Overview
question.scenario: Your company needs to establish a secure connection between your on-premises data center and Google Cloud VPC without using dedicated hardware.
question.question-text: What service provides encrypted connectivity between on-premises networks and GCP over the public internet?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need encrypted connectivity over the public internet between on-premises and GCP without dedicated physical links, look for the service that creates IPsec tunnels. This is the most common starting point for hybrid connectivity.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud VPN securely connects your on-premises network to your Google Cloud VPC through IPsec VPN tunnels over the public internet. Traffic is encrypted by one VPN gateway and decrypted by the other, providing confidentiality without dedicated hardware or private circuits. Option A (Cloud Router) provides BGP-based dynamic routing but is not a connectivity service by itself. Option C (VPC Peering) connects two GCP VPC networks, not on-premises to GCP. Option D (Cloud Interconnect) provides private dedicated connections that bypass the internet entirely, which requires physical infrastructure at a colocation facility or through a partner.

ul.li: GCP offers two Cloud VPN variants: Classic VPN supports a single tunnel with static or dynamic routing, while HA VPN provides two interfaces with automatic failover and a 99.99% SLA when both tunnels are configured. HA VPN is the recommended choice for production workloads.

Each VPN tunnel supports up to 3 Gbps of throughput (with proper MTU and packet size). To achieve higher aggregate bandwidth, you can create multiple tunnels and use ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) routing to distribute traffic across them.

Cloud VPN uses IKEv1 or IKEv2 for key exchange and supports AES-128/256-CBC and AES-128/256-GCM encryption. The peer VPN gateway must support compatible cipher suites and IKE versions for the tunnel to establish.

Cloud VPN is often the first step in hybrid connectivity, providing a quick-to-deploy encrypted link while organizations evaluate whether Cloud Interconnect is needed for higher bandwidth or lower latency requirements.

question.title: HA VPN Configuration
question.scenario: Your organization requires a highly available VPN connection with 99.99% uptime SLA between on-premises and Google Cloud.
question.question-text: What is required to achieve the 99.99% SLA with HA VPN?

choices.choice: Configure two VPN tunnels from HA VPN gateway to the peer gateway
Use Classic VPN with a single tunnel
Deploy the VPN gateway in multiple regions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The HA VPN SLA depends on redundancy. The gateway has two interfaces, and Google requires tunnels from both interfaces to your peer gateway for the availability guarantee to apply. A single tunnel does not qualify.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: HA VPN gateways have two interfaces, each with its own external IP address in a separate availability domain. To achieve the 99.99% SLA, you must configure VPN tunnels from both interfaces to your peer VPN gateway, ensuring redundancy if one tunnel or availability domain fails. Option B is wrong because Classic VPN does not offer an SLA at all. Option C is wrong because HA VPN gateways are regional resources and the SLA is achieved through dual-interface redundancy, not multi-region deployment. Option D sidesteps the question; Cloud Interconnect is a different service with its own SLA model.

ul.li: HA VPN exclusively uses dynamic routing with Cloud Router and BGP. Static routing is not supported with HA VPN, unlike Classic VPN which supports both. This ensures automatic failover between tunnels without manual route changes.

Each HA VPN interface connects to a different Google edge availability domain, providing infrastructure-level redundancy. If the peer gateway also has two interfaces, you can create four tunnels (2x2 full mesh) for maximum resilience.

Active/active configuration distributes traffic across both tunnels using ECMP for higher aggregate throughput. Active/passive configuration routes all traffic through one tunnel and fails over to the second only when the primary drops, using BGP MED or AS-path prepending.

The 99.99% SLA requires both tunnels to be configured and operational. If you configure only one tunnel on an HA VPN gateway, Google does not guarantee any SLA, and the setup provides no better availability than Classic VPN.

question.title: Cloud Router and BGP
question.scenario: You need dynamic route exchange between your on-premises network and GCP so that new subnets are automatically advertised.
question.question-text: What GCP service enables dynamic routing using BGP for hybrid connectivity?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Dynamic routing means routes are learned and advertised automatically via a routing protocol. In GCP, one specific service runs BGP sessions with your on-premises routers to exchange route information without manual configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Router is a fully distributed, software-defined router that uses the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to dynamically exchange routes between your VPC and connected networks. When new subnets are created in your VPC, Cloud Router automatically advertises them to on-premises, and it learns on-premises routes to install in the VPC routing table. Option A (Cloud NAT) provides outbound NAT for VMs without external IPs. Option B (Cloud VPN) provides the encrypted tunnel but relies on Cloud Router for dynamic routing. Option D (VPC Routes) are the routing table entries themselves, not a service that performs dynamic exchange.

ul.li: Cloud Router is required for HA VPN (which mandates dynamic routing) and is strongly recommended for Cloud Interconnect. It is a regional resource, but when global dynamic routing mode is enabled on the VPC, a Cloud Router in one region can advertise and learn routes for all regions.

Custom route advertisements let you override the default behavior and control exactly which routes are shared with on-premises. You can advertise specific prefixes, suppress default subnet routes, or advertise summary routes to reduce routing table size.

Cloud Router supports BGP communities and AS-path prepending for influencing route selection on the on-premises side. You assign a private ASN (64512-65534 or 4200000000-4294967294) to each Cloud Router instance.

Cloud Router also powers Cloud NAT by providing the regional control plane where NAT gateways are configured. Without Cloud Router, neither HA VPN, dynamic Interconnect routing, nor Cloud NAT can function.

question.title: Cloud Interconnect Options
question.scenario: Your company requires high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity to Google Cloud that doesn't traverse the public internet.
question.question-text: Which service provides dedicated, private connectivity to Google Cloud with higher bandwidth than VPN?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need private, high-bandwidth connections that bypass the public internet entirely, GCP offers a physical connectivity service with two deployment models depending on whether you can colocate at a Google edge facility or need a service provider.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Interconnect provides dedicated, private connectivity between on-premises networks and Google Cloud that does not traverse the public internet. Dedicated Interconnect offers 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps connections directly to Google at colocation facilities. Partner Interconnect provides connectivity through supported service providers for organizations that cannot colocate. Option A (VPC peering) connects GCP VPCs to each other, not on-premises networks. Option C is wrong because VPN tunnel bandwidth is capped at 3 Gbps per tunnel and always traverses the internet. Option D (Cloud CDN) is a caching service that does not provide private network connectivity.

ul.li: Dedicated Interconnect requires a physical cross-connect at one of Google's colocation facilities (e.g., Equinix, CoreSite). You provision 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits and can bundle multiple connections using link aggregation groups (LAGs) for higher capacity.

Partner Interconnect is available through approved service providers when your data center is not at a Google edge location. Bandwidth ranges from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps depending on the provider, and you can provision VLAN attachments in increments.

Both Interconnect types support VLAN attachments that connect the physical circuit to specific VPCs via Cloud Router. A single physical Interconnect connection can serve multiple VPCs and projects through separate VLAN attachments.

Cloud Interconnect traffic is not encrypted by default because it travels over private circuits. If encryption is required for compliance, you can layer HA VPN over Interconnect to add IPsec encryption while retaining private connectivity and bandwidth.

question.title: Dedicated vs Partner Interconnect
question.scenario: Your company is evaluating Cloud Interconnect options. You are not colocated at a Google edge facility but need more bandwidth than VPN provides.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Interconnect option should you choose when you cannot colocate at a Google edge facility?

choices.choice: Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When your data center is not physically present at a Google edge colocation facility, you need a third-party service provider to bridge the gap. GCP offers a specific Interconnect variant designed for exactly this scenario.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Partner Interconnect provides private connectivity to Google Cloud through supported service providers, making it ideal when your data center is not colocated at a Google edge facility. The partner handles the physical connection to Google, and you connect to the partner's network. Option A (Direct Peering) provides access to Google's public services but not private VPC access. Option B is misleading because Dedicated Interconnect requires physical presence at a Google colocation point. Option D (multiple VPN tunnels) traverses the public internet and has lower per-tunnel bandwidth, making it unsuitable when the requirement is private high-bandwidth connectivity.

ul.li: Partner Interconnect supports bandwidth from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps depending on the provider, with VLAN attachments provisioned in standard increments (50 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 200 Mbps, 500 Mbps, 1/2/5/10/20/50 Gbps). This flexibility lets you start small and scale up.

Partners operate as either Layer 2 or Layer 3 providers. Layer 2 partners pass VLAN tags transparently and you configure BGP directly between your router and Cloud Router. Layer 3 partners manage the BGP session on your behalf and you configure routing with the partner.

Partner Interconnect has a 99.9% SLA with a single VLAN attachment. To achieve 99.99% availability, deploy redundant VLAN attachments in two different edge availability domains, mirroring the HA VPN redundancy model.

Cost comparison: Dedicated Interconnect has lower per-GB egress charges but higher fixed costs (port fees, cross-connect fees). Partner Interconnect has lower fixed costs but higher per-GB rates. Break-even typically occurs around 1-2 TB/month of egress traffic.

question.title: VPC Peering
question.scenario: Your organization has two separate GCP projects that need to communicate using internal IP addresses without going through the public internet.
question.question-text: What feature allows two VPC networks to communicate using internal IP addresses?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When two VPC networks need direct internal IP communication without tunnels or gateways, GCP provides a peering mechanism that creates a low-latency, high-bandwidth link using Google's internal network fabric.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Network Peering allows two VPC networks to communicate using internal IP addresses, regardless of whether they are in the same project, different projects, or even different organizations. Traffic stays within Google's network and never traverses the public internet. Option A (Cloud VPN) creates encrypted tunnels typically for on-premises connectivity, which is unnecessary overhead for GCP-to-GCP communication. Option C (Cloud Interconnect) connects on-premises networks to GCP, not two GCP VPCs. Option D (external load balancing) exposes resources to the internet, defeating the purpose of internal communication.

ul.li: VPC Peering is non-transitive: if VPC-A peers with VPC-B and VPC-B peers with VPC-C, VPC-A cannot reach VPC-C through VPC-B. To achieve full connectivity you must create a direct peering between every pair of VPCs that need to communicate.

Peered VPC networks must have non-overlapping IP ranges for all subnets and secondary ranges. If any CIDR blocks overlap, the peering creation fails. This constraint makes IP address planning critical before establishing peering.

Peering exchanges subnet routes by default, but you can also export and import custom routes (static and dynamic) between peered VPCs. This is configured per-peering-connection and allows on-premises routes learned via Cloud Router to be shared across peered VPCs.

Each VPC network supports up to 25 peering connections by default (quota increase available). Peering provides full-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity with no per-GB charges for traffic between peered networks within the same region.

question.title: Shared VPC
question.scenario: Your organization wants multiple projects to share a common VPC network managed by a central network team while allowing project teams to manage their own resources.
question.question-text: What feature allows multiple projects to share a centrally managed VPC network?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP supports a centralized networking model where one project owns the VPC and other projects deploy their resources into it. This separates network administration from workload management, a key enterprise governance pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Shared VPC allows an organization to connect resources from multiple service projects to a common VPC network hosted in a designated host project. The network admin team manages the VPC, subnets, firewall rules, and routes in the host project, while service project teams deploy VMs, GKE clusters, and other resources using that shared network. Option B (VPC Peering) connects separate VPC networks rather than sharing one. Option C (Cloud Interconnect) connects on-premises networks to GCP. Option D (multiple VPCs per project) creates isolated networks within a single project, which is the opposite of centralized sharing.

ul.li: The host project contains the Shared VPC network and all its subnets, firewall rules, routes, and VPN/Interconnect connections. Service projects are attached to the host project and granted access to specific subnets via IAM roles (compute.networkUser or compute.subnetUser).

Shared VPC supports granular subnet-level permissions: a service project can be granted access to only specific subnets, enforcing network segmentation. For example, the dev team's project might only access the dev-subnet, while the prod team accesses prod-subnet.

Shared VPC requires an organization node in Cloud Identity or Google Workspace. The Shared VPC Admin role (compute.xpnAdmin) at the organization or folder level is needed to designate host projects and attach service projects.

Shared VPC is preferred over VPC Peering for enterprise landing zones because it provides centralized control with a single routing domain, simplifies firewall management, and avoids the non-transitive limitation of peering.

question.title: Private Google Access
question.scenario: Your VMs have only internal IP addresses but need to access Google Cloud APIs and services like Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: What feature allows VMs without external IPs to access Google APIs and services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: VMs without external IPs cannot reach the internet by default, but GCP offers a subnet-level setting that specifically enables access to Google APIs and services through Google's internal network without requiring a public IP address.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Google Access (PGA) allows VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, and Container Registry through Google's internal network. It is enabled at the subnet level. Option A (Cloud VPN) connects on-premises to GCP and does not help VMs reach Google APIs. Option B (Cloud NAT) provides general outbound internet access via NAT, which works but is broader than needed for Google API access and incurs NAT processing overhead. Option C (VPC Peering) connects two VPCs and does not provide access to Google services. PGA is the targeted, zero-cost solution specifically designed for this use case.

ul.li: Private Google Access must be enabled individually on each subnet where VMs need it. VMs with external IP addresses can access Google APIs regardless of this setting because they already have internet connectivity. PGA only affects VMs without external IPs.

PGA routes traffic to Google APIs through special IP ranges (199.36.153.4/30 for restricted, 199.36.153.8/30 for private). You can combine PGA with custom DNS entries for restricted.googleapis.com or private.googleapis.com to control which API endpoint is used.

For on-premises access to Google APIs over VPN or Interconnect (without going through the internet), use Private Google Access for on-premises, which requires DNS configuration to resolve Google API domains to the restricted or private VIP ranges.

Private Service Connect is a newer, more flexible alternative that creates dedicated endpoints with consumer-owned IP addresses in your VPC for accessing Google APIs, managed services, and third-party published services.

question.title: Cloud NAT
question.scenario: Your VMs need to download software updates from the internet but should not have external IP addresses for security reasons.
question.question-text: What service provides outbound internet connectivity for VMs without external IP addresses?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When VMs need general outbound internet access (not just Google APIs) without having public IPs, GCP provides a managed NAT service that translates internal source addresses to public addresses for outgoing connections only.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation) allows VMs without external IP addresses to initiate outbound connections to the internet, such as downloading software updates or reaching external APIs. It performs source NAT on outbound traffic while blocking unsolicited inbound connections, maintaining the security benefit of not having public IPs. Option A (Cloud VPN) connects to on-premises networks, not the general internet. Option C (Private Google Access) only provides access to Google APIs and services, not the broader internet. Option D (External Load Balancer) provides inbound traffic distribution and does not enable outbound internet access for backend VMs.

ul.li: Cloud NAT is software-defined and fully managed: it does not rely on a NAT VM instance or a single proxy. It scales automatically with traffic and provides high availability without user intervention. There is no single point of failure or bandwidth bottleneck.

Cloud NAT is configured on a Cloud Router and can apply to all subnets in a region or specific subnets only. You can also configure it to apply only to VMs without external IPs, to all VMs, or to specific subnet ranges.

NAT IP addresses can be automatically allocated or manually specified. Manual allocation is useful when external services require IP allowlisting. You can configure minimum ports per VM to ensure adequate connection capacity for high-throughput workloads.

Cloud NAT provides only outbound connectivity; it does not allow unsolicited inbound connections from the internet. This is a key security distinction from assigning external IPs, where inbound traffic is possible unless blocked by firewall rules.

question.title: Cloud DNS Overview
question.scenario: You need to manage DNS records for your domain and ensure high availability and low latency DNS resolution globally.
question.question-text: What Google Cloud service provides managed, authoritative DNS hosting?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Authoritative DNS means hosting the definitive DNS records for your domain so the world can resolve your domain names. GCP has a dedicated managed service for this, backed by Google's global anycast network for fast resolution.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud DNS is a high-performance, resilient, global DNS service that publishes your domain names to the global DNS using Google's infrastructure, offering a 100% SLA for authoritative name resolution. Option A (Cloud Domains) is a domain registration service for purchasing and managing domain names, not for hosting DNS records. Option B (Cloud CDN) caches web content at edge locations and has nothing to do with DNS record management. Option D (Cloud Load Balancing) distributes traffic across backends but does not host DNS zones or records. Cloud DNS supports both public zones for internet-facing records and private zones for internal VPC resolution.

ul.li: Cloud DNS supports public managed zones (resolvable from the internet), private managed zones (resolvable only within authorized VPC networks), forwarding zones (forward queries to on-premises DNS), and peering zones (delegate resolution to another VPC).

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) is supported for public zones to authenticate DNS responses and prevent spoofing attacks. Cloud DNS manages the key signing and zone signing automatically when DNSSEC is enabled.

Cloud DNS uses anycast name servers distributed globally, so DNS queries are answered by the nearest available name server. This provides consistently low-latency resolution regardless of where the query originates.

Cloud DNS supports all standard record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV, NS, SOA, PTR, CAA) and provides a programmable API for automated record management, making it suitable for dynamic environments using Infrastructure as Code tools like Terraform.

question.title: Private DNS Zones
question.scenario: You want to create internal DNS names for your VMs that are only resolvable within your VPC network.
question.question-text: What Cloud DNS feature provides DNS resolution only within specified VPC networks?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need DNS names visible only inside your VPC (like db.internal.example.com), you need a zone type that restricts resolution to authorized VPC networks. Public zones would expose these records to the entire internet.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private managed zones in Cloud DNS provide DNS records that are only resolvable from authorized VPC networks. They enable you to create internal hostnames like db.internal.example.com that are invisible to the public internet. Option A (forwarding zones) forward queries to external DNS servers rather than hosting records locally. Option B (public managed zones) make records resolvable by anyone on the internet, which defeats the purpose of internal-only names. Option C (peering zones) delegate resolution to another VPC's DNS configuration but do not host records themselves. Private zones are the correct choice for internal service discovery and private name resolution.

ul.li: Private zones can be attached to multiple VPC networks, including VPCs in different projects, using the authorized networks list. This enables centralized DNS management across Shared VPC or multi-project architectures.

When a private zone and a public zone both exist for the same domain, the private zone takes precedence for queries from authorized VPCs. This enables split-horizon DNS where internal clients resolve internal IPs and external clients resolve public IPs for the same domain.

Overlapping private zones are resolved using longest-suffix matching: a query for db.prod.internal.example.com would match a zone for prod.internal.example.com over a zone for internal.example.com, giving you fine-grained control over name resolution.

GCP automatically creates internal DNS records for VM instances in the format [instance-name].[zone].c.[project-id].internal. Private managed zones let you supplement this built-in DNS with custom, human-readable names for services and endpoints.

question.title: DNS Forwarding
question.scenario: Your hybrid environment requires VMs in GCP to resolve DNS names hosted on your on-premises DNS servers.
question.question-text: What Cloud DNS feature forwards DNS queries to on-premises or other DNS servers?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: In hybrid environments, some DNS names are managed by on-premises DNS servers. GCP needs a way to send queries for those specific domains to your on-premises servers rather than trying to resolve them through public DNS or local zones.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: DNS forwarding zones configure Cloud DNS to forward queries for specific domains to designated target name servers, such as your on-premises DNS infrastructure. When a VM in GCP queries a name in the forwarded domain, Cloud DNS sends the query over VPN or Interconnect to your on-premises DNS server for resolution. Option A (DNS peering zones) forward queries to another VPC's DNS configuration, not to external servers. Option B (private managed zones) host records locally within Cloud DNS. Option C (public managed zones) host internet-facing records. Forwarding zones are essential for hybrid DNS where on-premises names must be resolvable from GCP.

ul.li: Target name servers in forwarding zones can be on-premises DNS servers reachable via VPN or Interconnect, or external DNS servers on the internet. For on-premises targets, ensure the Cloud DNS source IP ranges (35.199.192.0/19) are allowed through your on-premises firewall.

For the reverse direction (on-premises resolving GCP private DNS names), configure a DNS Server Policy with inbound forwarding enabled. This creates inbound forwarder entry points with internal IP addresses that on-premises DNS servers can target as conditional forwarders.

Forwarding zones support two modes: default routing (use the VPC's standard routing to reach targets) and private routing (use the route of a specific VPC). Private routing is useful in Shared VPC environments where DNS traffic needs to follow a specific network path.

Combining forwarding zones with private zones creates a complete hybrid DNS architecture: private zones handle GCP-internal names, forwarding zones handle on-premises names, and public zones handle internet-facing names, all managed through Cloud DNS.

question.title: Cloud CDN Overview
question.scenario: Your web application serves static content to users worldwide and you want to reduce latency and origin server load.
question.question-text: What Google Cloud service caches content at edge locations to reduce latency for users?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A content delivery network caches frequently accessed content at locations close to end users, reducing the distance data must travel. GCP integrates its CDN service directly with the Global external Application Load Balancer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud CDN (Content Delivery Network) uses Google's globally distributed edge points of presence to cache HTTP/HTTPS content close to users, reducing latency, decreasing load on origin servers, and lowering egress costs. Option B (Cloud DNS) resolves domain names but does not cache content. Option C (Cloud Armor) provides DDoS protection and WAF capabilities but does not cache content. Option D (Cloud Storage) is an object storage service that can serve as an origin for cached content but does not itself cache at edge locations. Cloud CDN is enabled as a simple checkbox on a backend service attached to a Global external Application Load Balancer.

ul.li: Cloud CDN integrates exclusively with the Global external Application Load Balancer. You enable CDN on individual backend services or backend buckets, and Google's edge network automatically caches eligible responses at over 150 edge locations worldwide.

Cache keys determine how responses are stored and matched. By default the key includes the full URL, but you can customize it to include or exclude query parameters, host headers, and HTTP headers for fine-grained cache control.

Signed URLs and signed cookies provide time-limited, authenticated access to cached content. This enables CDN caching for premium or restricted content while preventing unauthorized access, commonly used for video streaming and software distribution.

Cache invalidation lets you purge specific cached objects or URL-prefix patterns when content changes. However, invalidation is not instant (propagates within minutes), so for time-sensitive updates, use versioned URLs (e.g., /style-v2.css) instead of relying on invalidation.

question.title: Cloud Armor Overview
question.scenario: Your public-facing web application needs protection against DDoS attacks and common web vulnerabilities like SQL injection.
question.question-text: What Google Cloud service provides DDoS protection and Web Application Firewall (WAF) capabilities?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: DDoS protection and WAF are Layer 7 security concerns that operate at the application edge. GCP provides a dedicated security service that sits in front of your Global external Application Load Balancer to filter malicious traffic before it reaches your backends.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Armor provides DDoS protection, WAF capabilities, and access control for applications served through the Global external Application Load Balancer. It includes preconfigured WAF rules based on the OWASP Top 10 (SQL injection, XSS, etc.) and supports custom rules using IP ranges, geographic locations, and request attributes. Option A (Cloud NAT) provides outbound NAT for VMs without external IPs. Option B (VPC Firewall Rules) operate at the network layer (Layer 3/4) and cannot inspect HTTP payloads for application-layer attacks. Option D (Identity-Aware Proxy) provides identity-based access control but does not offer DDoS mitigation or WAF capabilities.

ul.li: Cloud Armor security policies contain ordered rules evaluated by priority. Each rule specifies a match condition (IP range, geo location, or a CEL expression inspecting request headers and body) and an action (allow, deny with status code, throttle, or redirect).

Adaptive Protection uses machine learning to detect and mitigate Layer 7 DDoS attacks in real time. It analyzes traffic patterns, identifies anomalies, and can automatically suggest or apply rules to block attack traffic.

Rate limiting rules control the volume of requests from specific sources. You can configure rate-based banning (temporarily block sources exceeding a threshold) or throttling (return 429 responses when limits are exceeded), with granularity per IP or per header value.

Cloud Armor also supports bot management with reCAPTCHA Enterprise integration, allowing you to challenge suspicious clients before they reach your application. This is configured as a redirect action in security policy rules.

question.title: Cloud Armor Security Policies
question.scenario: You need to block traffic from specific countries and rate limit requests to your API endpoints while allowing legitimate traffic.
question.question-text: What component of Cloud Armor defines the rules for allowing or denying traffic?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Armor organizes its traffic filtering logic into a specific resource type that contains an ordered list of rules. Each rule has a match condition and an action, evaluated from highest priority to lowest until a match is found.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Armor security policies contain rules evaluated in priority order (lower number = higher priority). Each rule defines a match condition (IP ranges, geographic location, custom CEL expressions) and an action (allow, deny, throttle, redirect). The first matching rule determines the action taken on the request. Option A (network tags) are used for VPC firewall rule targeting, not Cloud Armor. Option B (VPC firewall rules) operate at Layer 3/4 and cannot filter by country or rate-limit HTTP requests. Option D (IAM policies) control access to GCP resources and APIs, not HTTP traffic to load-balanced applications. Security policies are attached to backend services on the Global external Application Load Balancer.

ul.li: Rules support the Common Expression Language (CEL) for complex matching, allowing conditions like request.headers['user-agent'].contains('bot') or origin.region_code == 'CN'. CEL expressions can inspect headers, cookies, URI paths, query parameters, and request body.

Geo-based rules use IP geolocation to identify the source country or region. A common pattern is to create a default deny rule and add explicit allow rules for approved countries, implementing a geographic allowlist for compliance requirements.

Rate limiting rules support two enforcement actions: throttle (respond with 429 Too Many Requests while continuing to allow some traffic) and rate-based ban (block the source entirely for a configurable ban duration once the threshold is exceeded).

Every security policy must have a default rule at the lowest priority (2147483647). This rule applies to traffic that does not match any other rule, and it can be set to allow or deny. Setting the default to deny implements a positive security model.

question.title: Identity-Aware Proxy
question.scenario: You want to control access to your internal web applications based on user identity rather than network location.
question.question-text: What Google Cloud service provides context-aware access control for applications without a VPN?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The BeyondCorp zero-trust model replaces VPN-based network perimeters with identity-based access controls. GCP implements this model through a proxy service that authenticates users before granting access to applications.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) controls access to cloud applications and VMs based on user identity and context (device security posture, location, time of day) rather than network location. Users are authenticated through Google identity services, enabling BeyondCorp-style zero-trust access without requiring a VPN. Option B (Cloud Armor) provides DDoS and WAF protection but does not authenticate users. Option C (VPC Service Controls) creates security perimeters around GCP services to prevent data exfiltration, operating at the API layer rather than the user-application layer. Option D (Cloud VPN) provides encrypted network tunnels, which is the traditional perimeter-based approach that IAP is designed to replace.

ul.li: IAP works with App Engine, Compute Engine (via load balancer), GKE, and on-premises applications connected through IAP Connector. It intercepts HTTPS requests, verifies user identity with Google's OAuth 2.0 flow, and checks IAM permissions before allowing access.

Access Context Manager integration enables context-aware policies that consider device attributes (OS version, encryption status, screen lock), IP address, geographic location, and time of access. This lets you enforce rules like "allow only from managed devices during business hours."

IAP supports TCP forwarding for SSH and RDP access to VMs without bastion hosts or public IPs. The gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap command establishes an encrypted tunnel through IAP, authenticating the user and checking IAM permissions before granting access.

IAP passes authenticated user identity to backends via signed headers (X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email, X-Goog-Authenticated-User-ID), enabling applications to know who is making requests without implementing their own authentication layer.

question.title: VPC Service Controls
question.scenario: You need to prevent data exfiltration from sensitive Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Cloud Storage, even by authorized users.
question.question-text: What feature creates security perimeters around Google Cloud services to prevent data exfiltration?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Even users with proper IAM permissions could copy data to an unauthorized project or external bucket. GCP provides a service that draws security boundaries around projects and services, preventing data from leaving the perimeter regardless of user permissions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Service Controls define security perimeters around Google Cloud resources to prevent data exfiltration. Even with proper IAM permissions, data cannot move outside the perimeter unless explicitly allowed through ingress/egress policies. This protects against both external attackers and insider threats. Option A (Private Google Access) enables VMs to reach Google APIs without external IPs but does not restrict where data can flow. Option C (Cloud Armor) protects against DDoS and web attacks at the load balancer layer. Option D (VPC Firewall Rules) control network traffic at Layer 3/4 but cannot restrict API-level data movement between projects or organizations.

ul.li: Service perimeters protect specific GCP services (BigQuery, Cloud Storage, GKE, Pub/Sub, Spanner, and many others). Resources inside a perimeter can communicate freely, but cross-perimeter access is blocked unless explicit ingress/egress policies are defined.

Access Context Manager works with VPC Service Controls to define access levels based on IP address, device attributes, and identity. For example, you can allow perimeter access only from specific corporate IP ranges or managed devices.

Dry-run mode lets you test perimeter configurations by logging violations without enforcing them. This is critical for evaluating the impact of a new perimeter on existing workflows before activating enforcement, preventing accidental service disruptions.

Perimeter bridges enable controlled communication between two perimeters for cross-project data sharing scenarios. Ingress/egress rules can specify which projects, services, identities, and methods are allowed to cross the perimeter boundary.

question.title: Routes and Routing
question.scenario: You need to understand how traffic flows from VMs in your VPC to destinations on the internet and other networks.
question.question-text: What determines the path that network traffic takes from a VM to its destination?

choices.choice: Routes in the VPC routing table

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Every VPC has a routing table that tells the network fabric where to send packets based on their destination IP address. Routes define the next hop for each destination, determining the physical path packets take through the network.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Routes in the VPC routing table determine the path network packets take from VM instances to their destinations. The routing table contains system-generated routes (automatically created for subnet ranges and default internet gateway) and custom routes (static routes you create or dynamic routes learned via Cloud Router/BGP). Option A (network tags) are labels used to scope firewall rules and routes to specific VMs but do not define routing paths themselves. Option C (firewall rules) control whether traffic is allowed or denied but do not determine the path it takes. Option D (service accounts) provide identity for VMs and are used for IAM authorization, not routing decisions.

ul.li: System-generated routes are created automatically: a subnet route for each subnet's CIDR range (directing traffic to VMs within the subnet) and a default route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to the default internet gateway. These routes cannot be deleted but the default route can be replaced.

Custom static routes let you define explicit next hops for specific destination ranges. Next hop types include VM instances, internal load balancers, VPN tunnels, default internet gateways, and IP addresses. This enables traffic steering through virtual network appliances.

Dynamic routes are learned from Cloud Router via BGP and are automatically installed in the routing table. In regional dynamic routing mode, routes apply only to the region where the Cloud Router resides. In global mode, routes propagate to all regions in the VPC.

When multiple routes match a destination, GCP selects the most specific route (longest prefix match). If two routes have equal specificity, priority determines the winner. For equal-priority equal-specificity routes, ECMP distributes traffic across the next hops.

question.title: Custom Static Routes
question.scenario: You need to route traffic destined for a specific IP range through a network virtual appliance (firewall VM) in your VPC.
question.question-text: What type of route should you create to direct traffic through a specific VM instance?

choices.choice: Custom static route with next hop as the VM instance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need to steer traffic through a specific VM (such as a firewall appliance or NAT instance), you must create a route that explicitly names that VM as the next hop for the target destination range.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Custom static routes allow you to define explicit routing paths with specific next hop targets. By setting the next hop to a VM instance, you force all traffic matching the destination range to pass through that VM, enabling inspection, filtering, or transformation by a virtual appliance. Option B (system-generated subnet routes) are auto-created for local subnet ranges and cannot be customized. Option C (default internet gateway route) sends traffic to the internet and cannot be redirected to a VM. Option D (VPC peering routes) are automatically exchanged between peered VPCs and cannot be manually pointed at a VM. Custom static routes are the standard mechanism for implementing hub-and-spoke network appliance architectures.

ul.li: Next hop types for custom static routes include: instance (specific VM by name and zone), internal load balancer (for high availability), VPN tunnel, default internet gateway, and IP address. Using an internal LB as next hop is preferred for production because it provides failover if the appliance VM goes down.

Routes can be scoped to specific VMs using network tags. For example, a route with tag "needs-inspection" and next hop pointing to a firewall VM will only affect VMs with that tag, while other VMs use the default routing path. This enables selective traffic steering.

The target VM must have IP forwarding enabled (canIpForward=true) to process packets not destined for its own IP address. Without IP forwarding, the VM drops packets that do not match its own network interface IPs.

More specific routes (longer CIDR prefix) always take precedence over less specific ones. A /24 route to a firewall VM overrides the default /0 internet route for that specific range, ensuring targeted traffic inspection without affecting all outbound traffic.

question.title: Health Checks
question.scenario: Your load balancer is sending traffic to unhealthy backend instances, causing user errors.
question.question-text: What load balancer component determines whether backend instances can receive traffic?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Load balancers need to know which backends are healthy before routing traffic to them. A dedicated probing mechanism periodically tests each backend and removes unhealthy ones from the serving pool until they recover.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Health checks periodically probe backend instances to verify they can serve traffic. Instances failing health checks are marked unhealthy and removed from the load balancing pool, preventing users from being routed to broken backends. Supported protocols include HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP/2, TCP, SSL, and gRPC. Option B (firewall rules) control whether traffic is permitted but do not assess backend health. Option C (URL maps) define routing rules but do not monitor backend status. Option D (SSL certificates) enable HTTPS termination but have no bearing on whether a backend is operational. The scenario describes a likely misconfigured or missing health check.

ul.li: Health check parameters include check interval (how often probes are sent), timeout (how long to wait for a response), healthy threshold (consecutive successes to mark healthy), and unhealthy threshold (consecutive failures to mark unhealthy). Tuning these values balances detection speed against false positives.

Health check probes originate from Google's dedicated IP ranges: 130.211.0.0/22 and 35.191.0.0/16. VPC firewall rules must explicitly allow ingress from these ranges to the health check port on your backends, or probes will be blocked and all backends will appear unhealthy.

For HTTP/HTTPS health checks, you can specify the request path (e.g., /healthz), expected response codes, and response content to match. This enables application-level health verification beyond simple TCP connectivity, catching scenarios where a VM is running but the application is broken.

Health checks are also used by Managed Instance Groups for autohealing. When a VM fails the MIG health check, the autohealer automatically deletes and recreates the instance, providing self-healing infrastructure without manual intervention.

question.title: SSL/TLS Termination
question.scenario: You want to offload SSL/TLS encryption from your backend servers to reduce their CPU load.
question.question-text: At what point does the Global external Application Load Balancer terminate SSL/TLS connections by default?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: SSL termination refers to where encrypted connections are decrypted. The default behavior for Application Load Balancers is to handle encryption at the frontend, relieving backend servers of the computational cost of TLS handshakes and encryption.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Global external Application Load Balancer terminates SSL/TLS at the load balancer frontend by default. Client connections are encrypted between the user and the load balancer, which handles the TLS handshake and decryption. Traffic from the load balancer to backends travels over Google's internal network and can use HTTP or HTTPS depending on your configuration. Option B is wrong because backends do not perform TLS termination by default in this architecture. Option C is wrong because CDN edge locations serve cached content but the load balancer handles TLS. Option D is incorrect as SSL/TLS is a core capability of the Application Load Balancer.

ul.li: GCP supports three certificate types: Google-managed certificates (automatically provisioned and renewed via ACME/Let's Encrypt, zero operational overhead), self-managed certificates (you upload your own cert and key), and Certificate Manager certificates (for advanced certificate lifecycle management).

End-to-end encryption is possible by configuring HTTPS as the protocol between the load balancer and backends. This adds a second TLS session from the LB to each backend, ensuring data is encrypted in transit even on Google's internal network, which may be required for compliance.

SSL policies control which TLS versions (1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3) and cipher suites are available. The RESTRICTED profile allows only TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers, while COMPATIBLE supports older clients. Custom profiles let you enable specific cipher suites.

A single load balancer frontend can host up to 15 SSL certificates using Server Name Indication (SNI), allowing multiple domains to share one IP address. Clients that do not support SNI are served the primary (first) certificate.

question.title: Network Endpoint Groups
question.scenario: You want to load balance traffic directly to containers in GKE without going through a NodePort service.
question.question-text: What resource type allows load balancers to target individual pods or containers directly?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Container-native load balancing requires a backend type that can reference individual pod IP addresses rather than node-level endpoints. GCP provides a resource that groups IP:port pairs representing specific containers or services.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs) are collections of IP:port endpoints that can represent individual pods, VMs, or external services. Container-native load balancing uses zonal NEGs to route traffic directly to GKE pods via their pod IPs, bypassing kube-proxy and NodePort, which improves latency and enables accurate health checking per pod. Option B (Instance Groups) target VM instances, not individual containers. Option C (Target Pools) are a legacy resource for Network Load Balancers. Option D (Backend Buckets) serve static content from Cloud Storage buckets. NEGs are the modern, flexible backend type for container and microservice architectures.

ul.li: Zonal NEGs are used for GCE VMs and GKE pods within a specific zone. When used with GKE, the NEG controller automatically registers and deregisters pod endpoints as pods scale up/down, keeping the load balancer's backend list synchronized with the cluster state.

Internet NEGs (also called hybrid NEGs) reference endpoints outside GCP, such as on-premises servers or services in other clouds. This enables GCP's Global Application Load Balancer to front multi-cloud or hybrid architectures from a single entry point.

Serverless NEGs point to Cloud Run, App Engine, or Cloud Functions services, allowing the Application Load Balancer to route to serverless backends alongside VM and container backends in the same URL map.

Container-native load balancing with NEGs provides pod-level health checking: the load balancer probes each pod individually rather than the node, ensuring traffic is only sent to healthy pods. This eliminates the double-hop latency of NodePort and provides more precise load distribution.

question.title: VPN Tunnel Configuration
question.scenario: You are setting up Cloud VPN and need to ensure that traffic for your on-premises network (10.0.0.0/8) routes through the VPN tunnel.
question.question-text: How are routes for on-premises networks typically configured with HA VPN?

choices.choice: Configured in the on-premises firewall only
Automatically detected by the VPN gateway
Dynamically through BGP sessions with Cloud Router
Manually created as static routes for each tunnel

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: HA VPN mandates dynamic routing, which means routes are not manually configured on the GCP side. Instead, a routing protocol session runs between the Cloud Router and your on-premises router to automatically exchange reachability information.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: HA VPN requires dynamic routing through Cloud Router using BGP. Routes for on-premises networks (like 10.0.0.0/8) are learned through BGP sessions established between the Cloud Router and the on-premises router, and VPC subnet routes are advertised back to on-premises. This eliminates manual route management and ensures routes update automatically when network changes occur. Option A is wrong because routing must be configured on both sides. Option C is wrong because VPN gateways do not auto-detect remote networks. Option D describes static routing, which is only available with Classic VPN and is not supported by HA VPN.

ul.li: Classic VPN supports both static and dynamic routing, but HA VPN exclusively requires dynamic routing via BGP. This design decision ensures that failover between the two HA VPN tunnels happens automatically through BGP convergence rather than requiring manual route updates.

BGP ASN (Autonomous System Number) must be configured on both Cloud Router and the on-premises router. Cloud Router uses a private ASN (16-bit: 64512-65534, or 32-bit: 4200000000-4294967294). The on-premises router can use its own private or public ASN.

Custom route advertisements on Cloud Router let you control exactly which routes are shared with on-premises. You can suppress default subnet advertisements and instead advertise summary routes, specific prefixes, or routes from peered VPCs to simplify the on-premises routing table.

BGP session health directly impacts the VPN tunnel status. If the BGP session drops, the tunnel is considered down and traffic fails over to the remaining healthy tunnel. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) can be enabled for faster failure detection (sub-second).

question.title: Internal IP Addresses
question.scenario: You need a VM's internal IP address to remain the same even if the VM is deleted and recreated.
question.question-text: What type of internal IP address should you reserve for this requirement?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: IP addresses in GCP can be either ephemeral (temporary, released when the resource is deleted) or static (reserved, persists independently of any resource). To keep the same internal IP across VM lifecycle events, you need the static variant.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Static internal IP addresses are reserved within a subnet and persist independently of VM instances. When a VM is deleted, a static internal IP remains reserved in the subnet and can be reassigned to a new VM, ensuring services that depend on that IP address continue to work. Option A (ephemeral internal IP) is automatically released when the VM is deleted, so the new VM would get a different IP. Option B (external IP) provides a public internet-facing address, not an internal VPC address. Option D (alias IP) provides additional IPs on a VM's network interface for containers or services but is not the mechanism for preserving a VM's primary internal IP across recreations.

ul.li: Static internal IPs are regional resources tied to a specific subnet. When reserving, you specify the subnet and optionally the exact IP address from that subnet's CIDR range. If you do not specify an address, GCP picks an available one from the subnet range.

Reserved static internal IPs incur charges when they are not attached to a running VM instance. This pricing encourages releasing unused reservations and helps prevent IP address hoarding in large organizations.

Common use cases for static internal IPs include database servers (where application connection strings reference a fixed IP), internal DNS entries that must remain stable, and load balancer forwarding rules that serve as well-known service endpoints.

Alias IP addresses are distinct from static IPs: they assign additional IP ranges to a VM's network interface from secondary subnet ranges. They are used for running multiple services or containers on a single VM, not for ensuring a primary IP persists across VM lifecycle events.

question.title: External IP Addresses
question.scenario: Your VM needs to be accessible from the internet, but you want the IP address to persist across VM stops and starts.
question.question-text: What type of external IP should you use for a VM that needs a persistent public IP?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Ephemeral external IPs may change when a VM is stopped and restarted. For a public IP that must remain the same across VM lifecycle events, you need to reserve a static external IP and assign it to the VM's network interface.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Static external IP addresses are reserved and remain assigned to a VM even when stopped and restarted. Ephemeral external IPs may change when a VM is stopped, which breaks DNS records, firewall allowlists, and client configurations that reference the old IP. Option A (ephemeral) does not persist across stop/start cycles. Option B (Cloud NAT) provides shared outbound NAT IPs that you do not directly assign to a VM, and the NAT IP is not the VM's own address. Option D (load balancer IP) provides a stable frontend IP but requires a full load balancer setup for a single VM, adding unnecessary complexity and cost when you just need a persistent public IP on one instance.

ul.li: Static external IPs come in two tiers: Premium tier IPs are global resources that use Google's premium backbone network for optimal routing, while Standard tier IPs are regional and route traffic through the public internet with potentially higher latency.
