Premium tier is required for global load balancers and provides anycast addresses. Standard tier is cheaper and suitable for regional workloads where global routing optimization is unnecessary.

Unused static external IPs (reserved but not assigned to a running resource) incur hourly charges to discourage IP address hoarding. This is especially important to monitor in organizations with many projects, as orphaned reservations accumulate cost.

For VMs that must be internet-accessible but need automatic IP management, consider putting them behind a load balancer with a static frontend IP instead. This provides the stable IP, adds health checking and SSL termination, and allows scaling to multiple backends later.

question.title: Hierarchical Firewall Policies
question.scenario: Your organization wants to enforce consistent firewall rules across all projects while allowing project teams some flexibility.
question.question-text: What feature allows you to define firewall rules at the organization or folder level?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP's resource hierarchy (organization, folders, projects) allows security controls to be applied at higher levels and inherited downward. Firewall policies at the organization or folder level enforce baselines that individual project teams cannot override.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Hierarchical firewall policies allow you to create and enforce firewall rules at the organization or folder level, providing consistent security baselines across all projects within that scope. Rules can allow traffic, deny traffic, or delegate the decision to the next lower level using the goto_next action. Option A (Cloud Armor) operates at the load balancer layer for HTTP traffic, not at the network layer across all projects. Option C (VPC firewall rules) are defined per-VPC within a project and cannot enforce organization-wide policies. Option D (network tags) are VM-level labels used for rule targeting, not a policy enforcement mechanism. Hierarchical policies are evaluated before VPC-level rules in the firewall evaluation order.

ul.li: Firewall rule evaluation follows the hierarchy top-down: organization policy rules are evaluated first, then folder policy rules, then VPC network firewall rules. At each level, rules are evaluated by priority. The goto_next action passes the decision to the next level, enabling delegation.

A common pattern is to enforce a deny-all rule for known malicious IP ranges at the organization level, use goto_next for most traffic to delegate to project-level rules, and add explicit allow rules at the org level for critical shared services like health check probes.

Hierarchical policies use the same rule syntax as VPC firewall rules (direction, priority, match conditions, action) but add the goto_next action. They also support targeting specific VPC networks within the scope, so a folder-level policy can apply different rules to different VPCs.

Managing hierarchical firewall policies requires the compute.orgSecurityPolicyAdmin role at the organization or folder level. This role is intentionally separate from project-level compute.securityAdmin to enforce separation of duties between network security teams and project teams.

question.title: Managed Instance Groups
question.scenario: You want to automatically scale the number of web server VMs based on traffic load behind a load balancer.
question.question-text: What GCP feature provides auto-scaling and auto-healing for groups of identical VMs?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need a fleet of identical VMs that automatically grows or shrinks based on demand and self-heals when instances fail, GCP provides a managed compute primitive that handles instance lifecycle based on a template you define.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) create and manage groups of identical VM instances from an instance template. MIGs support autoscaling (adjusting instance count based on metrics), autohealing (recreating failed instances based on health checks), and automated rolling updates (gradually replacing instances with a new template). Option B (Unmanaged Instance Groups) are collections of heterogeneous VMs without automation; they do not support autoscaling or autohealing. Option C (Network Endpoint Groups) are backend types for load balancers that reference IP:port pairs, not VM management constructs. Option D (Target Pools) are a legacy load balancer backend resource with limited features.

ul.li: Regional MIGs (also called multi-zone MIGs) distribute instances across multiple zones within a region, providing automatic zone-level redundancy. If one zone experiences an outage, the MIG maintains capacity in the remaining zones, which is critical for high-availability architectures.

The autoscaler adjusts MIG size based on CPU utilization, load balancer serving capacity, Cloud Monitoring custom metrics, or a schedule. You configure minimum and maximum instance counts and a cooldown period to prevent rapid oscillation during traffic spikes.

Autohealing uses a health check (separate from load balancer health checks) to detect unhealthy instances. When an instance fails the health check for the configured unhealthy threshold, the autohealer deletes it and creates a replacement from the instance template.

Rolling updates allow you to change the instance template (e.g., new machine image, different machine type) and gradually replace instances. You control the update strategy: maximum surge (extra instances during update), maximum unavailable, and whether to use proactive or opportunistic replacement.

question.title: Cloud CDN Cache Modes
question.scenario: You want fine-grained control over which responses are cached by Cloud CDN and for how long.
question.question-text: What determines how Cloud CDN decides whether to cache a response?

choices.choice: Only the file extension of the request
Time of day the request is made
Cache mode settings and cache headers from origin

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud CDN caching decisions are driven by a combination of the cache mode you configure on the backend service and the HTTP cache-control headers your origin server sends. Neither file extension alone nor user location determines cacheability.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud CDN caching is controlled by the cache mode setting on the backend service and the cache headers (Cache-Control, Expires) returned by the origin server. The three cache modes determine how strictly origin headers are respected: CACHE_ALL_STATIC caches common static content types automatically, USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS requires valid cache headers from the origin, and FORCE_CACHE_ALL caches all successful responses regardless of headers. Option B is wrong because file extension is only one factor in CACHE_ALL_STATIC mode and is irrelevant in other modes. Option C is wrong because geographic location affects which edge node serves the cache but not whether content is cached. Option D has no bearing on caching decisions.

ul.li: CACHE_ALL_STATIC automatically caches responses with common static MIME types (images, CSS, JS, fonts, video) even if the origin does not send Cache-Control headers. This is the simplest mode for static websites and is the default for new backend services.

USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS requires the origin to send valid Cache-Control: public, max-age=N or s-maxage=N headers. Responses without these headers or with Cache-Control: private/no-store are not cached. This mode gives the origin full control over caching behavior.

FORCE_CACHE_ALL caches all HTTP 200/206 responses regardless of origin headers, using a configurable default TTL. Use this mode cautiously because it can cache personalized or sensitive content. It is most appropriate for origins that serve entirely public, non-personalized content.

You can set default TTL, maximum TTL, and client TTL on each backend service to override or cap the TTL values from origin headers. Negative caching (caching 404 and other error responses briefly) reduces origin load from repeated requests for missing resources.

question.title: VLAN Attachments
question.scenario: You have a Dedicated Interconnect connection and need to connect it to multiple VPC networks in different projects.
question.question-text: What resource connects a Cloud Interconnect connection to a VPC network?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A Cloud Interconnect connection is a physical circuit. To map that physical link to a specific VPC network and establish BGP routing, you need a logical resource that associates a VLAN on the circuit with a Cloud Router in the target VPC.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VLAN attachments (InterconnectAttachments) are the logical resource that connects a Cloud Interconnect connection to a Cloud Router in a specific VPC network. Each attachment allocates a VLAN ID on the physical circuit and establishes a BGP session with Cloud Router for route exchange. Multiple VLAN attachments can share a single Interconnect connection, enabling different VPCs and projects to use the same physical link. Option A (network peering) connects two VPCs but cannot bridge a physical Interconnect to a VPC. Option B (Cloud Router) handles BGP routing but is not the resource that binds the Interconnect to the VPC. Option C (VPN tunnel) creates encrypted tunnels over the internet, which is a different connectivity mechanism.

ul.li: Each VLAN attachment has a unique 802.1Q VLAN ID and is associated with exactly one Cloud Router in one VPC. The BGP session between Cloud Router and your on-premises router runs within that VLAN, exchanging routes specific to that VPC and its peered networks.

A single Dedicated Interconnect connection can support multiple VLAN attachments to different VPCs, different projects, or even different organizations. Each attachment gets its own BGP session, IP allocation, and bandwidth allocation from the shared physical circuit.

VLAN attachment bandwidth can be configured from 50 Mbps to the full port speed (10 or 100 Gbps for Dedicated Interconnect). For Partner Interconnect, the partner provisions the attachment with bandwidth tiers agreed upon in your service contract.

For redundancy, deploy VLAN attachments across two different Interconnect connections in different edge availability domains. This ensures that a single facility or circuit failure does not disconnect your VPC from on-premises, achieving the 99.99% SLA for Dedicated Interconnect.

question.title: Private Service Connect
question.scenario: You want to access Google APIs and third-party services using private IP addresses without sending traffic over the internet.
question.question-text: What feature provides private connectivity to Google and third-party services using internal IPs?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: While Private Google Access enables basic API access for VMs without external IPs, a more advanced feature creates dedicated endpoints with consumer-owned IP addresses in your VPC for reaching Google APIs, managed services, and third-party published services.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Service Connect (PSC) allows you to create private endpoints in your VPC that provide connectivity to Google APIs, Google-managed services, and third-party published services. Each endpoint gets an internal IP address from your VPC subnet, and traffic stays within Google's network. Option A (VPC Peering) connects two VPCs but cannot connect to Google-managed services or third-party providers. Option B (Private Google Access) enables basic API access but uses Google's VIP ranges rather than consumer-owned IPs, and does not support third-party services. Option D (Cloud NAT) provides outbound internet connectivity and does not create private service endpoints. PSC is the most flexible and modern approach to private service consumption.

ul.li: PSC endpoints are internal IP addresses allocated from a subnet in your VPC. When you create a PSC endpoint for Google APIs, you get a single IP that can resolve all Google API domains (storage.googleapis.com, bigquery.googleapis.com, etc.), simplifying DNS and firewall configuration.

PSC supports a producer/consumer model: service producers publish their services through PSC service attachments, and consumers create PSC endpoints or backends to access them. This enables third-party SaaS providers to offer private connectivity to their services without VPC peering.

PSC endpoints can be accessed from on-premises networks via VPN or Interconnect, enabling private access to Google APIs and published services from outside GCP. This eliminates the need for on-premises traffic to traverse the public internet to reach Google services.

PSC backends integrate with load balancers, allowing you to place PSC endpoints behind an internal Application Load Balancer for centralized access control, monitoring, and URL-based routing to different published services from a single entry point.

question.title: Firewall Logs
question.scenario: You need to troubleshoot connectivity issues and want to see which firewall rules are allowing or blocking traffic.
question.question-text: What feature provides visibility into firewall rule actions on network traffic?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When troubleshooting connectivity, you need to see exactly which firewall rule matched each connection and whether it allowed or denied the traffic. GCP has a dedicated logging feature for firewall rules that records this decision for every connection.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firewall Rules Logging records every connection that was evaluated by a firewall rule, including which rule matched, whether traffic was allowed or denied, source and destination IPs, ports, and protocol. This is the definitive tool for understanding why specific traffic is being blocked or permitted. Option A (Cloud Trace) is an application performance tracing service for distributed systems. Option B (VPC Flow Logs) capture traffic metadata (bytes, packets, IPs) for network monitoring but do not show which firewall rule acted on the traffic. Option D (Cloud Audit Logs) record API calls and administrative actions (who created/modified a rule) but not the real-time traffic decisions made by those rules.

ul.li: Firewall logging is enabled per individual firewall rule and generates a log entry for each connection that matches that rule. Enabling logging on high-traffic rules can generate significant log volume and associated Cloud Logging costs, so enable it selectively during troubleshooting.

Each log entry includes the rule name, action (ALLOW/DENY), direction (INGRESS/EGRESS), source/destination IPs and ports, protocol, and the VM instance that the rule was applied to. This makes it straightforward to trace exactly why a specific connection was blocked.

VPC Flow Logs and Firewall Rules Logging serve complementary purposes: Flow Logs capture all traffic metadata for network monitoring and analysis regardless of rule matches, while Firewall Logs specifically show rule-level allow/deny decisions. Use both together for comprehensive network visibility.

For interactive troubleshooting, the Connectivity Tests tool (Network Intelligence Center) performs reachability analysis without sending actual packets, checking routing and firewall configuration to determine whether a hypothetical connection would succeed. This is faster than enabling logs and waiting for test traffic.

question.title: VPC Flow Logs
question.scenario: Your security team needs to monitor network traffic patterns and detect anomalies across your VPC.
question.question-text: What feature captures metadata about IP traffic flowing through VPC network interfaces?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For broad network traffic monitoring and anomaly detection, you need a feature that captures metadata about all IP flows through VM network interfaces, not just traffic matched by specific firewall rules. This data enables traffic analysis, forensics, and compliance reporting.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic (source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, bytes, packets, timestamps) flowing to and from VM network interfaces. They provide comprehensive network visibility for monitoring, forensics, security analysis, and capacity planning. Flow Logs are enabled at the subnet level. Option A (Firewall Rules Logging) only records traffic matched by specific firewall rules, not all flows. Option B (Cloud Trace) is an application-level distributed tracing service for latency analysis. Option D (Cloud Profiler) analyzes application CPU and memory usage. VPC Flow Logs are the correct tool for network-level traffic pattern analysis.

ul.li: Flow Logs are configurable with sampling rate (0.0 to 1.0) and aggregation interval (5 seconds to 15 minutes). A lower sampling rate and longer aggregation interval reduce log volume and cost but provide less granular data. For security monitoring, a higher sampling rate is recommended.

Each flow log record includes source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, bytes transferred, packets transferred, start/end timestamps, and the VM instance name. When GKE is running on the VMs, log records also include pod name, namespace, and service information for Kubernetes-aware analysis.

Flow Logs integrate natively with BigQuery for large-scale analysis (e.g., identifying top talkers, detecting port scans, measuring cross-zone traffic) and with third-party SIEM tools like Splunk, Sumo Logic, and Chronicle for security monitoring and alerting.

Flow Logs capture metadata only, not packet payloads. For deep packet inspection (analyzing actual packet contents for malware or intrusion signatures), use Packet Mirroring instead, which copies full packets to a collector for analysis by IDS/IPS tools.

question.title: Session Affinity
question.scenario: Your application stores session data locally on web servers and requires users to return to the same backend instance.
question.question-text: What load balancer feature ensures requests from the same client are sent to the same backend?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When applications maintain local session state, the load balancer must consistently route a given client to the same backend instance. This is achieved through a stickiness mechanism that remembers client-to-backend mappings across multiple requests.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Session affinity (sticky sessions) ensures that requests from the same client are consistently directed to the same backend instance for the duration of a session. The Application Load Balancer supports several affinity types: client IP affinity (based on source IP), generated cookie affinity (using a load balancer-generated cookie), and header/cookie-based affinity (using an application-specified header or cookie). Option A (health checks) determine backend availability, not routing consistency. Option B (URL maps) route by URL path or host, not by client identity. Option D (connection draining) allows existing connections to complete during backend removal, which is a lifecycle concern not a routing concern.

ul.li: Client IP affinity hashes the source IP to select a backend. It works for all protocols but can cause uneven distribution when many clients share a single IP (NAT, corporate proxies). It is the simplest option and works with Network Load Balancers as well.

Generated cookie affinity (GENERATED_COOKIE) uses a cookie set by the load balancer to track client-to-backend mappings. This provides more accurate per-client affinity than IP-based methods and works correctly even when clients share IPs, but it requires cookie support in the client.

Best practice is to design stateless backends that store session data in external stores (Memorystore, Cloud SQL, Firestore). Stateless backends eliminate the need for session affinity, enabling better load distribution, simpler scaling, and graceful handling of backend failures.

Session affinity is a best-effort mechanism: if the target backend becomes unhealthy or is removed, the load balancer routes the client to a different healthy backend. Applications relying on affinity should handle session reconstruction gracefully for this scenario.

question.title: Packet Mirroring
question.scenario: Your security team needs to capture and analyze full packet payloads for intrusion detection without impacting production traffic.
question.question-text: What feature allows you to copy network traffic to a collector for analysis?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Deep packet inspection for intrusion detection requires access to actual packet contents, not just flow metadata. GCP provides a traffic cloning feature that copies full packets to a collector appliance without affecting the original traffic flow or adding latency.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Packet Mirroring clones traffic from specified sources (individual VMs, subnets, or network-tagged instances) and sends full packet copies to a collector deployed behind an internal load balancer. Unlike VPC Flow Logs, which capture only metadata, Packet Mirroring captures complete packet contents including payloads, enabling deep packet inspection for intrusion detection, forensics, and compliance. Option B (VPC Flow Logs) captures flow metadata (IPs, ports, bytes) but not packet payloads. Option C (Firewall Rules Logging) records rule-level allow/deny decisions. Option D (Cloud IDS) is a managed intrusion detection service that itself uses Packet Mirroring internally, but the question asks about the underlying traffic copying feature.

ul.li: Mirroring policies support fine-grained filtering by protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP), IP address ranges (source and/or destination), and traffic direction (ingress, egress, or both). This lets you mirror only the traffic relevant to your security analysis, reducing collector load and storage costs.

The collector is typically an internal load balancer fronting a pool of IDS/IPS appliances, packet analyzers, or SIEM collectors. Using a load balancer distributes mirrored traffic across multiple analysis tools for scalability and redundancy.

Packet Mirroring operates at the hypervisor level and does not affect the performance, latency, or throughput of the mirrored source traffic. The cloned packets are an out-of-band copy, so production workloads are completely unimpacted by the mirroring process.

Cloud IDS (Intrusion Detection System) uses Packet Mirroring under the hood to feed traffic to Palo Alto Networks threat detection engines. If you need managed threat detection without deploying your own analysis tools, Cloud IDS is the turnkey alternative to raw Packet Mirroring.

question.title: Direct Peering vs Cloud Interconnect
question.scenario: You need to access Google Workspace and YouTube with lower latency but don't need private connectivity to your VPC.
question.question-text: Which connectivity option provides direct access to Google's public services without private VPC access?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you only need better performance to Google's public services (like Workspace, YouTube, or Google Search) and do not require private access to your VPC resources, there is a BGP peering option that connects your network directly to Google's edge.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Direct Peering establishes a BGP peering connection between your network and Google's edge network at one of Google's peering locations. It provides optimized paths to Google's public services (Google Workspace, YouTube, Google Cloud APIs via public endpoints) but does not provide private access to your GCP VPC resources. Option A (Private Service Connect) creates private endpoints within your VPC for accessing services. Option C (Cloud VPN) creates encrypted tunnels to your VPC but does not optimize access to Google's public services specifically. Option D (Cloud Interconnect) provides private VPC connectivity, which is more than what is needed here. Direct Peering is free but has no SLA.

ul.li: Direct Peering is a free service with no SLA, no support from Google Cloud, and no integration with the GCP console. It requires meeting Google's peering technical requirements (public ASN, minimum traffic thresholds) and is established at one of Google's 100+ peering locations globally.

For organizations that cannot meet Google's peering requirements or lack presence at a peering location, Carrier Peering provides a similar service through an ISP partner. The ISP handles the peering relationship with Google and provides the last-mile connection to your network.

Neither Direct Peering nor Carrier Peering provides private access to VPC resources or integration with Cloud Router, VPN, or Interconnect. They exclusively optimize the path to Google's public-facing services and are completely separate from GCP networking.

The decision framework for hybrid connectivity: Direct/Carrier Peering for public Google service access only, Cloud VPN for encrypted VPC connectivity over internet, Partner Interconnect for private VPC connectivity without colocation, and Dedicated Interconnect for maximum bandwidth and lowest latency with colocation.

question.title: Global vs Regional Load Balancing
question.scenario: You are deploying an application that will only serve users in a single geographic region and want the most cost-effective load balancing option.
question.question-text: When should you choose a regional load balancer instead of a global load balancer?

choices.choice: When traffic is localized to one region and you want lower costs
When you need automatic multi-region failover
When you need content-based routing globally
When you need anycast IP addresses

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Global load balancers use the Premium network tier with anycast IPs and charge accordingly. When your application serves users in a single region with backends in that same region, a regional load balancer using Standard tier provides the same functionality at lower cost.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Regional load balancers are the right choice when your backends are in a single region and your users are geographically concentrated nearby. They cost less than global load balancers because they use the Standard network tier instead of Premium, and they do not require the overhead of global anycast infrastructure. Option A (multi-region failover) requires a global load balancer that can detect regional failures and redirect traffic. Option B (anycast IPs) are a global load balancer feature using Premium tier. Option C (global content-based routing) requires the Global external Application Load Balancer. Regional load balancers are ideal for internal applications, regionally-focused services, and cost-conscious workloads that do not need global reach.

ul.li: The Regional external Application Load Balancer uses the Standard network tier, where traffic is routed to the nearest Google PoP via the public internet rather than entering Google's premium backbone at the edge. Standard tier has lower egress costs but may have higher latency for distant users.

The Global external Application Load Balancer uses the Premium network tier with anycast IPs that enter Google's backbone at the nearest edge PoP, providing optimal routing globally. Premium tier has higher egress costs but delivers better performance and enables features like Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor.

Internal load balancers (both Application and Network variants) are always regional resources regardless of network tier. For internal-only traffic between services in the same region, regional internal LBs are the natural and most cost-effective choice.

GCP also offers a Cross-region internal Application Load Balancer for organizations that need internal Layer 7 routing across multiple regions. This is a newer product that bridges the gap between regional internal and global external load balancing for multi-region internal architectures.

question.title: DNS Peering
question.scenario: You have a Shared VPC setup and want service projects to use DNS zones defined in the host project.
question.question-text: What Cloud DNS feature allows one VPC to use private DNS zones from another VPC?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: In multi-VPC architectures, private DNS zones hosted in one VPC need to be accessible from other VPCs. Cloud DNS provides a zone type that delegates resolution for specific domains from a consumer VPC to a producer VPC that hosts the authoritative zone.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: DNS peering zones allow a consumer VPC network to forward DNS queries for specific domains to a producer VPC network that hosts the authoritative private zone. This enables centralized DNS management in Shared VPC or multi-VPC architectures where one VPC maintains the master DNS records and other VPCs query them through peering. Option A (DNS forwarding zones) forward queries to external name servers (like on-premises DNS), not to another VPC's Cloud DNS. Option B (cross-project binding) is not a Cloud DNS feature. Option C (public managed zones) are internet-facing and do not address private cross-VPC resolution. DNS peering is the correct mechanism for sharing private DNS across VPC boundaries.

ul.li: The producer VPC hosts private managed zones with authoritative records. Consumer VPCs create DNS peering zones that point to the producer VPC for specific domains. When a VM in the consumer VPC queries a name in the peered domain, Cloud DNS transparently resolves it using the producer VPC's zone data.

DNS peering is transitive: if VPC-A peers to VPC-B for domain.example.com, and VPC-B has a forwarding zone that sends domain.example.com queries to an on-premises DNS server, VPC-A's queries will follow the chain through VPC-B to on-premises. This enables hub-and-spoke DNS architectures.

Setting up DNS peering requires the dns.peer role on the target (producer) network. The peering is configured in the consumer VPC's Cloud DNS, specifying the target VPC network. No configuration change is needed on the producer side beyond granting the IAM permission.

In Shared VPC environments, the host project's VPC typically hosts all private zones, and service project VPCs (if they have separate VPCs) use DNS peering to resolve names from the host. Alternatively, if service projects use subnets in the Shared VPC directly, they inherit DNS resolution without needing peering.

question.title: Cloud IDS
question.scenario: You need managed network-based threat detection that integrates with your existing security tools.
question.question-text: What Google Cloud service provides managed intrusion detection for network threats?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need a managed, turnkey intrusion detection system that analyzes network traffic for malware, exploits, and command-and-control activity without deploying your own IDS appliances, GCP offers a service powered by Palo Alto Networks threat intelligence.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud IDS is a managed intrusion detection service that analyzes mirrored network traffic for threats using Palo Alto Networks threat detection technology. It identifies malware, spyware, command-and-control attacks, vulnerability exploits, and other network-based threats without requiring you to deploy or manage IDS appliances. Option A (VPC Service Controls) prevents data exfiltration at the API level, not network-level threat detection. Option B (Cloud Armor) provides DDoS and WAF protection at the load balancer layer for HTTP traffic. Option C (Packet Mirroring) is the underlying traffic copying mechanism that Cloud IDS uses, but it does not itself analyze traffic for threats. Cloud IDS provides the complete detection pipeline: traffic capture, analysis, and alerting.

ul.li: Cloud IDS uses Packet Mirroring internally to capture and analyze traffic without inline inspection, meaning it does not add latency to production traffic. Traffic is copied to Google-managed Palo Alto Networks virtual appliances that perform deep packet analysis against known threat signatures.

Threat findings from Cloud IDS are reported to Security Command Center (SCC), Cloud Logging, and can be forwarded to third-party SIEM and SOAR platforms. This integration enables automated incident response workflows, such as triggering Cloud Armor rules to block attacker IPs.

Cloud IDS provides threat intelligence from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, including continuously updated signatures for known malware variants, CVE exploits, and threat actor techniques. The signature database is updated automatically without customer intervention.

Cloud IDS endpoints are regional resources deployed in specific zones. Each endpoint monitors traffic from selected subnets in the same region. For full VPC coverage, you need Cloud IDS endpoints in every region where you have workloads, and mirroring policies configured for the relevant subnets.

question.title: Network Connectivity Center
question.scenario: You have multiple branch offices connected via VPN and want to enable branch-to-branch communication through Google's network.
question.question-text: What service provides hub-and-spoke connectivity for hybrid and multi-cloud networks?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When multiple branch offices or clouds need to communicate with each other through Google's backbone network rather than through individual point-to-point links, GCP provides a hub-and-spoke networking service that treats Google's network as a transit backbone.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Network Connectivity Center (NCC) is a hub-and-spoke model for network connectivity management that enables site-to-site data transfer through Google's global network. It connects VPN tunnels, Interconnect attachments, and SD-WAN router appliances as spokes in a unified topology, allowing any-to-any communication between connected sites. Option A (Shared VPC) shares a single VPC across projects but does not provide transit connectivity between on-premises sites. Option B (VPC Peering) connects two VPCs but does not enable branch-to-branch transit. Option D (Cloud Router) handles BGP routing for individual connections but does not orchestrate a hub-and-spoke transit network. NCC turns Google Cloud into a WAN backbone connecting distributed sites.

ul.li: NCC spokes can be HA VPN tunnels, VLAN attachments (Interconnect), or third-party SD-WAN router appliances running on Compute Engine. Each spoke connects a site (branch office, data center, or cloud region) to the NCC hub, and the hub enables any-to-any routing between all connected spokes.

Site-to-site data transfer through NCC uses Google's global backbone network, providing enterprise-grade performance, reliability, and security for inter-site traffic. This eliminates the need to build and maintain dedicated MPLS or SD-WAN overlay networks between branch offices.

NCC supports both first-party spokes (GCP VPN and Interconnect) and third-party spokes (SD-WAN appliances from vendors like Cisco, Palo Alto, and Fortinet). This enables existing SD-WAN deployments to leverage Google's backbone as a transport layer.

NCC also supports VPC spokes for connecting multiple VPC networks within GCP in a hub-and-spoke model. This provides an alternative to full-mesh VPC Peering for organizations with many VPCs that need centralized routing and transit connectivity.

question.title: Connection Draining
question.scenario: You need to remove a backend instance from the load balancer pool for maintenance without abruptly terminating active user sessions.
question.question-text: What feature allows existing connections to complete before removing a backend from service?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When removing a backend for maintenance, you want existing in-flight requests to finish gracefully rather than being terminated mid-response. GCP load balancers provide a feature that stops sending new requests to the backend while allowing active connections to complete within a timeout.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Connection draining allows existing connections to a backend to complete gracefully when the backend is removed from the serving pool due to scaling down, rolling updates, health check failures, or manual removal. New connections are immediately routed to other healthy backends, but in-progress connections continue on the draining backend until they complete or the draining timeout expires. Option A (capacity scaler) adjusts the proportion of traffic a backend receives but does not manage connection lifecycle during removal. Option C (health checks) detect unhealthy backends but do not control how existing connections are handled during removal. Option D (session affinity) routes clients to the same backend but does not address graceful removal scenarios.

ul.li: The draining timeout is configurable per backend service, with a default of 300 seconds (5 minutes) and a maximum of 3600 seconds (1 hour). When the timeout expires, any remaining connections to the draining backend are terminated. Set the timeout based on your application's typical request duration.

Connection draining works seamlessly with MIG rolling updates: as instances are replaced with a new template, the old instances enter draining state, allowing in-flight requests to complete before the instances are deleted. This enables zero-downtime deployments for stateful workloads.

For WebSocket connections and long-lived streaming connections, the draining timeout must be set high enough to accommodate the expected connection duration. HTTP/2 multiplexed streams are individually drained, so new streams are refused while existing streams complete.

Connection draining is distinct from graceful shutdown at the application level. Ideally, both work together: the load balancer stops sending new requests (draining), and the application handles SIGTERM by finishing in-progress work and closing connections cleanly.

term.name: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
term.definition: A global, private, isolated virtual network in Google Cloud that provides networking functionality for your resources.
term.exam-note: VPCs are global; subnets are regional. Resources in the same VPC can communicate via internal IPs.

term.name: Subnet
term.definition: A regional resource that defines an IP address range within a VPC network from which VM instances receive their internal IP addresses.
term.exam-note: Subnets are regional and must have non-overlapping IP ranges within a VPC.

term.name: VPC Firewall Rule
term.definition: A rule that allows or denies traffic to/from VM instances based on configuration including direction, priority, targets, sources, and protocols.
term.exam-note: Ingress is denied by default; egress is allowed by default. Lower priority number means higher precedence.

term.name: Cloud NAT
term.definition: A managed network address translation service that enables instances without external IPs to access the internet for outbound connections.
term.exam-note: Cloud NAT is software-defined, highly available, and configured on Cloud Router.

term.name: Cloud VPN
term.definition: A service that provides encrypted IPsec VPN tunnels between your on-premises network and Google Cloud VPC over the public internet.
term.exam-note: HA VPN provides 99.99% SLA with two tunnels; requires dynamic routing with Cloud Router.

term.name: Cloud Interconnect
term.definition: A service that provides dedicated, private connectivity between on-premises networks and Google Cloud, bypassing the public internet.
term.exam-note: Dedicated Interconnect requires colocation; Partner Interconnect uses a service provider.

term.name: Cloud Router
term.definition: A fully distributed, software-defined router that uses BGP to dynamically exchange routes between your VPC and connected networks.
term.exam-note: Required for HA VPN and dynamic routing with Cloud Interconnect.

term.name: Cloud Load Balancing
term.definition: A suite of load balancing services that distribute traffic across backend resources based on type (global/regional, external/internal, protocol).
term.exam-note: Global Application LB for HTTP(S); Network LB for TCP/UDP; Internal LB for private traffic.

term.name: Cloud DNS
term.definition: A high-performance, resilient, global Domain Name System (DNS) service that publishes domain names to the global DNS.
term.exam-note: Supports public zones (internet), private zones (VPC only), and forwarding zones (hybrid).

term.name: Cloud CDN
term.definition: A content delivery network that caches HTTP(S) content at Google's globally distributed edge points of presence.
term.exam-note: Integrates with Global Application Load Balancer; supports cache invalidation and signed URLs.

term.name: Cloud Armor
term.definition: A DDoS protection and Web Application Firewall (WAF) service that protects applications behind Global Application Load Balancer.
term.exam-note: Security policies contain prioritized rules for allow, deny, throttle, or redirect actions.

term.name: Private Google Access
term.definition: A subnet-level setting that allows VMs without external IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services using internal IPs.
term.exam-note: Enable on subnets where VMs need Google API access without external IPs.

term.name: VPC Network Peering
term.definition: A feature that connects two VPC networks for internal IP communication, whether in the same project or different projects/organizations.
term.exam-note: Peering is non-transitive and requires non-overlapping IP ranges.

term.name: Shared VPC
term.definition: A feature that allows multiple projects (service projects) to use a common VPC network hosted in a host project.
term.exam-note: Centralizes network management while allowing distributed resource deployment.

term.name: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
term.definition: A service that controls access to applications based on user identity and context rather than network location.
term.exam-note: Enables BeyondCorp zero-trust access without VPN; supports TCP forwarding for SSH/RDP.
